name: DuckDB
summary: An in-process analytical SQL database: a library with no server that queries Parquet, CSV, Iceberg and S3 directly.
intro: DuckDB runs inside your process, the way SQLite does, but it’s built for analytics: columnar storage and a vectorised engine that works on batches of values in parallel threads, spilling to disk when a query outgrows memory. It has no external dependencies and installs as a library for Python, R, Java or Node.js, or as a single command-line binary. A database is one file, or you can skip that and query files where they are: `SELECT ... FROM 's3://bucket/*.parquet'`.

Extensions add formats and storage. `httpfs` reads and writes S3 and HTTP; `iceberg` reads Iceberg tables and writes them through a REST catalog; `delta` reads and writes Delta Lake using the Delta Kernel library; `postgres` queries a live PostgreSQL database; and `ducklake` attaches DuckLake catalogs. The current release is 1.5.6, and the 1.4 line (1.4.5) is the long-term support release.
strengths: Zero setup: `pip install duckdb` and you have a fast columnar engine
Reads Parquet, CSV, JSON, Iceberg and Delta Lake in place, locally or on S3, reading only the columns and row groups it needs
Larger-than-memory queries spill to disk, so one laptop or VM goes a long way
MIT licensed, with the IP held by the non-profit DuckDB Foundation
limits: One machine only: it scales up, not out
Only one process can write to a database file at a time; it isn’t a shared server for many users
Iceberg writes need a REST catalog; reading a table by its path is read-only
Built for analytics, not many small transactional writes; use PostgreSQL or SQLite for app data

story: By the late 2010s, a data scientist with a few gigabytes in R or pandas had two poor options. A database server meant installing, configuring and loading data through a slow client protocol. SQLite ran inside the program with no setup, but it was built for transactions, with a row-by-row engine over B-trees, so analytical queries ran very slowly. The dataframe tools themselves offered relational-style operators but no query optimiser.

Mark Raasveldt and Hannes Mühleisen, database researchers at CWI in Amsterdam, had already built MonetDBLite, an embedded version of the MonetDB analytical database. It was popular, used from the Dutch central bank to the New Zealand police, but adapting a system that wasn’t built for embedding caused problems that were hard to fix. In 2018 they started again from scratch: a purpose-built analytical database that runs inside another program, as SQLite does. They presented DuckDB at SIGMOD 2019 in Amsterdam, MIT licensed from the start.

In 2021 the founders spun off a company from CWI, DuckDB Labs, to employ the core engineering team, and set up the non-profit DuckDB Foundation to hold most of the IP. DuckDB 1.0 arrived in June 2024 with a file format that later versions promise to keep reading. In May 2026 DuckDB Labs renamed itself DuckLabs. In August 2026 DuckLabs announced it would join AWS as a new subsidiary, expected to take effect in early September; DuckDB, DuckLake and Quack stay MIT licensed under the stewardship of the DuckDB Foundation.

choices.choice: Run inside the host process, like SQLite
choices.why: An embedded library needs no server, and because the database and application share memory, tables can move between DuckDB and pandas or R without being copied over a socket.

choices.choice: A columnar, vectorised engine instead of SQLite’s row engine
choices.why: Analytical queries touch a few columns across many rows. Processing columns in batches of values uses the CPU far better than handling one row at a time.

choices.choice: No external dependencies, and never crash the host
choices.why: MonetDBLite taught them that depending on external libraries caused trouble and that an embedded database that crashes takes the user’s program down with it. Queries that run out of memory must abort cleanly.
